title: Greedy Two Pointers on Height Arrays
summary: Converging pointers guided by a greedy safety proof on height and skyline arrays — the technique behind Container With Most Water and Trapping Rain Water.

slides.markdown:
Two classic problems — Container With Most Water and Trapping Rain Water — both work on an array of heights, both look like they need checking every pair or every position against its neighbors, and both collapse to a single O(n) two-pointer pass once you find the right **greedy safety argument**.

Unlike the [sorted pair-sum pattern](opposite-end-two-pointers), nothing here is sorted — heights can be in any order. The convergence is justified instead by a proof that a specific pointer move can never make the answer worse. Finding that proof, not the code, is the actual interview skill in this topic.

slides.subTitle: Why the shorter wall is always safe to move
slides.markdown:
Given an array of heights representing vertical walls, find two walls that, together with the x-axis distance between them, hold the most water: `area = min(height[left], height[right]) * (right - left)`.

Start `left` at 0, `right` at the last index. At each step, the **shorter** wall is the bottleneck — it's the one limiting how much water this pair can hold. Moving the taller wall inward can only shrink the width while the height limit stays capped by the same shorter wall (or gets worse if the new wall is even shorter). So moving the taller wall can never improve on the current pair.

Moving the **shorter** wall, though, shrinks the width too, but it's the only move that has any chance of finding a *taller* limiting wall next time — which is the only way area could possibly increase. So: always advance the pointer at the shorter wall.

slides.sectionTitle: Container With Most Water in one pass
slides.markdown:
```python
def max_area(height):
    left, right = 0, len(height) - 1
    best = 0
    while left < right:
        width = right - left
        h = min(height[left], height[right])
        best = max(best, h * width)
        if height[left] < height[right]:
            left += 1
        else:
            right -= 1
    return best
```

Every iteration computes the area for the current pair, updates the best seen, then advances whichever side is shorter (ties can move either — moving `right` here is an arbitrary but valid choice). The loop runs at most n-1 times, each doing O(1) work, for O(n) total — versus the O(n²) brute force of checking every pair of walls directly.

slides.sectionTitle: Assuming moving the taller wall could ever help
slides.markdown:
It's tempting to think "maybe the taller wall is blocking a better pair further in" and move it instead — this is wrong, and worth being able to prove, not just assert.

Suppose `height[left] < height[right]` and you move `right` inward instead of `left`. The new width is strictly smaller. The new area is `min(height[left], height[new_right]) * new_width`. Since `height[left]` was already the limiting height, the new area is bounded by `height[left] * new_width`, which is strictly less than `height[left] * old_width` — the area you already had. **No matter what height sits at the new right position**, moving the taller wall cannot produce a better result than the current pair. It can only tie or lose.

This is the proof that justifies the greedy choice — without it, "move the shorter wall" is just a rule you're trusting, not one you understand.

slides.subTitle: Water above a cell depends on the shorter of both max walls
slides.markdown:
Trapping Rain Water asks how much water sits on top of a height array after rain, where water is trapped between taller bars on both sides. The water level above index `i` is bounded by **the shorter of the tallest wall to its left and the tallest wall to its right** — `min(leftMax(i), rightMax(i)) - height[i]`, floored at zero.

This is a different question from Container With Most Water — there you pick exactly two walls; here, *every* index between two tall enough walls can hold water, and the relevant height at each position is a running maximum, not just the immediate neighbor.

The brute-force version recomputes `leftMax` and `rightMax` for every index by scanning outward each time — O(n²). The two-pointer version reuses the same greedy insight as Container With Most Water: you don't need both max values everywhere at once if you can prove which side's contribution is already determined.

slides.subTitle: Left-max and right-max closing in
slides.markdown:
Track `leftMax` and `rightMax` as running maximums seen so far from each side, and two pointers `left`/`right` converging inward. At each step, compare `height[left]` to `height[right]`: whichever side is **shorter** is the side whose water level is fully determined right now, because the taller side guarantees a wall at least that high exists somewhere — so process that side and advance its pointer.

For `height = [0,1,0,2,1,0,1,3]`: as `left` and `right` converge, whenever `height[left] < height[right]`, water above `left` is `leftMax - height[left]` (since the eventual right wall is guaranteed at least `height[right] ≥ leftMax` isn't needed — only that it's taller than `left`'s side). Symmetric logic applies when the right side is shorter.

slides.sectionTitle: Trapping Rain Water with two pointers and O(1) space
slides.markdown:
```python
def trap(height):
    left, right = 0, len(height) - 1
    left_max, right_max = 0, 0
    water = 0
    while left < right:
        if height[left] < height[right]:
            left_max = max(left_max, height[left])
            water += left_max - height[left]
            left += 1
        else:
            right_max = max(right_max, height[right])
            water += right_max - height[right]
            right -= 1
    return water
```

When `height[left] < height[right]`, that guarantees some wall at least `height[right]`'s height exists to the right — so the water above `left` is safely determined by `left_max` alone, regardless of what's further right. This is O(n) time and O(1) extra space, compared to O(n) time but O(n) space for the precomputed-arrays version, or O(n²) time for the brute-force rescan-every-index version.

slides.sectionTitle: Two-pointer trapping vs precomputed max arrays vs a monotonic stack
slides.markdown:
Trapping Rain Water has three standard solutions with different space profiles for the same O(n) time:

| Approach | Time | Space | Idea |
|---|---|---|---|
| Brute force | O(n²) | O(1) | Rescan left and right for every index |
| Precomputed leftMax/rightMax arrays | O(n) | O(n) | Two passes fill arrays, one pass sums water |
| Two pointers | O(n) | O(1) | Greedy: process the shorter side, whose water level is already determined |
| Monotonic stack | O(n) | O(n) worst case | Fill water layer-by-layer between bars using a decreasing stack of indices |

The two-pointer version is the space-optimal O(n) solution and the one worth defaulting to. The monotonic-stack version is worth mentioning because it generalizes better to a 2D variant (Trapping Rain Water II), where two pointers no longer apply cleanly and a priority queue over the boundary takes over instead.

slides.sectionTitle: Why the greedy proof matters more than the code here
slides.markdown:
Both problems in this topic look, on the surface, like the sorted-array convergence from earlier topics — two pointers closing in, one line of comparison logic deciding which one to move. But there's no sorted order anywhere in a height array; the justification for convergence is entirely a **greedy exchange argument**: showing that the move you didn't make is provably no better than the one you did.

That's a meaningfully different kind of proof than "the array is sorted, so this comparison is monotonic." A senior candidate distinguishes the two explicitly: sorted-input two pointers are correct because of a structural guarantee about the data; greedy height-array two pointers are correct because of a local exchange argument that has to be re-derived for each new problem — it doesn't transfer automatically just because the shape (converging pointers on an array) looks similar.

When you hit a new height-array-style problem, the right first move is asking "what's the exchange argument here?" — not "which pointer usually moves in these problems?"

slides.sectionTitle: Recognizing greedy two pointers on skylines
slides.markdown:
The signal for this pattern: an array of heights or capacities, a question about area, volume, or a max/min pairing across positions, and a naive solution that checks all pairs or rescans on every index. Before coding, ask whether one side of a comparison is provably "locked in" — a value that, once compared, cannot benefit from being reconsidered later.

This closes out the converging-pointer half of the group: opposite ends on sorted arrays, matching two sequences, same-direction compaction, kSum extensions, and now greedy exchange arguments on height arrays. The rest of the group turns to a related but distinct family — sliding windows, where both pointers move in the **same** direction across a single sequence to track a contiguous subrange rather than converging toward each other.
